lessons.t: Why more ideas beat one good idea
lessons.intro: You will learn why producing a large number of rough ideas gives better results than polishing the first one. It matters because your best idea is rarely your first.

cards.b: Early ideas are usually obvious. The more you produce, the more likely a few unusual ones appear. Many breakthroughs come from the tenth or twentieth option, not the first.
If you evaluate each idea as it appears, you stop generating new ones. Separate the two phases, produce first and judge later, so the stream keeps moving.
Set a target such as 20 ideas in 10 minutes. The target pushes you past the obvious answers into less familiar territory where new ideas live.

fig.title: Ideas kept, by round
fig.note: Later rounds often produce the strongest ideas.

ex.q: A team lists 4 ideas in round one and 12 in round two. How many ideas do they have in total?
ex.why: Add the two rounds: 4 plus 12 equals 16. Every round adds to the pool you choose from, so the total is 16 ideas.

lessons.tip: Write down the weak ideas too, because they often point toward good ones.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to generate many ideas before judging any?
quiz.why: Judging early interrupts idea generation, so separating the phases keeps more options coming.

quiz.q: Which situation shows the value of quantity?
o: Only one idea is needed by noon
The first idea is always best
Twenty options are listed before choosing
Ideas are cut before being written
quiz.why: A larger pool gives you more chances to find an unusual, strong option.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to chain words together to reach ideas you would not reach directly. It matters because it gives you a fast, structured way to wander away from the obvious.

cards.b: Write the word that describes your problem in the centre of a page. Then write the first word that comes to mind next to it, without checking whether it is relevant.
Take the last word you wrote and free associate again. Repeat five or six times, because each step drifts a little further from the starting point.
The words at the end of a chain are the most unusual. Pick one and ask how it relates to your problem, since this connection is often where the surprising idea sits.

fig.title: A five-step word chain
fig.note: Each word links to the one before it.

ex.q: A cafe wants more morning customers. Its word chain is Coffee, Steam, Cloud, Rain. Which word is the fourth in the chain?
ex.why: Count the chain: Coffee is first, Steam second, Cloud third and Rain fourth. The far end of a chain is where the most distant links appear, so Rain is the word to explore next.

lessons.tip: Set a two-minute timer so the chain keeps moving without pauses.

quiz.q: What should you do when a free-association word seems irrelevant?
o: Keep it and continue the chain
quiz.why: Irrelevant words can be the link to a surprising idea, so keep them and continue.

quiz.q: Where are the most unusual links usually found in a word chain?
quiz.why: Each step drifts further from the start, so the last words are the most distant.

lessons.intro: You will learn to use a fixed set of standard questions to unlock new ideas about any problem. It matters because a good question opens doors that staring at the problem never will.

cards.b: Use a fixed set of questions for every problem. Consistency helps you compare answers and notice the gaps you would otherwise miss.
Ask who else could use this, when it could be used, and where it could happen. Changing the setting often reveals a new purpose for the same product.
Push the problem into extremes. What if it cost nothing? What if it had to be finished in one hour? Impossible conditions force unusual thinking.

fig.title: The question stack
fig.note: Work down the list for each problem.

ex.q: A team uses the question stack on a water bottle. It asks 4 questions per idea and generates 5 ideas. How many questions in total?
ex.why: Each idea gets four questions, so the team asks 4 questions for each of the 5 ideas. Four times five equals 20 questions in total.

lessons.tip: Write the answer to each question on its own line so none get lost.

quiz.q: Why use the same questions for every problem?
o: To avoid the what if question
To compare answers and spot gaps
quiz.why: Consistent questions make answers comparable and reveal what you have not yet considered.

quiz.q: What does the what if question do?
quiz.why: Extreme conditions, such as zero cost, force unusual thinking that normal conditions do not.

lessons.t: Reversing the problem to find ideas
lessons.intro: You will learn how to flip a problem around and ask how to make it worse. It matters because reversed questions often reveal the causes you need to fix.

cards.b: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how you could guarantee failure. This makes the causes of the problem easy to list.
Take each cause of failure and reverse it. If meetings always run late, the reversed idea is to set a firm start time and keep the agenda short.
Not every reversal is useful, but many point to simple fixes. Keep the ones that address a real cause and drop the rest.

fig.title: Direct versus reversed thinking
fig.note: Reversal finds causes that direct questions miss.

ex.q: A cafe lists 3 causes of long queues, and each cause adds 5 minutes of waiting. How many minutes of delay do the causes add in total?
ex.why: Three causes of 5 minutes each add up to 15 minutes. Adding the three delays gives the total, which is what the reversed question helps you attack.

lessons.tip: Reverse the problem first, then reverse the answers to find practical fixes.

quiz.q: What is the aim of asking how to make a problem worse?
o: To list the causes of the problem
To prove the problem is fake
quiz.why: Asking how to fail makes the causes of the problem easy to name, and causes are where fixes begin.

quiz.q: Meetings always run late. Which idea is a reversed fix?
o: Set a firm start and short agenda
quiz.why: A firm start and a short agenda reverse the cause of lateness, while the other options would make lateness worse.

lessons.intro: You will learn to use an unrelated word as a jolt to shift your thinking. It matters because random prompts break the habits of thought that keep you stuck.

cards.b: Open a book and point at a random word without looking. Choose a noun that has nothing to do with your problem, such as lamp or river.
List three features of the random word, such as its shape, its use or its colour. Each feature gives you a new angle to apply to the problem.
Ask how each feature could become part of your solution. A river that carries things might suggest a conveyor, and that could solve a packing problem.

fig.title: Stimulus word loop
fig.note: Repeat the loop with a new word each time.

ex.q: You pick the word river and list 3 traits. For each trait you create 4 linked ideas. How many linked ideas do you have in total?
ex.why: Three traits times four ideas each gives 12 linked ideas. Each trait opens a fresh set of possibilities to test.

lessons.tip: Keep a notebook of random words so you can reuse them on future problems.

quiz.q: Why choose a word unrelated to your problem?
quiz.why: An unrelated word forces a new angle, which helps you escape familiar patterns.

quiz.q: A river that carries items suggests what for a packing problem?
quiz.why: The carrying trait of a river can be linked to a conveyor that moves items along.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to set a numeric target for an idea session and track your progress. It matters because a clear number keeps you going past the first comfortable answers.

cards.b: Decide how many ideas you want before you start, such as 30. A target stops you settling early and gives the session a clear finish.
Count ideas in batches of ten. Seeing the count rise is motivating, and you can tell when you are slowing down and need a new prompt.
The first ten ideas are usually the most obvious. Ideas from the last third of the session are often the most original, so keep going.

fig.title: Unusual ideas per ten
fig.note: Unusual ideas rise as the session goes on.

ex.q: A team sets a target of 30 ideas. After 20 ideas have been listed, how many more ideas do they need to reach the target?
ex.why: The target is 30 and 20 ideas already exist. Subtracting 20 from 30 leaves 10 more ideas to generate.

lessons.tip: Set the target slightly higher than feels comfortable.

quiz.q: Why set a number before brainstorming?
quiz.why: A target pushes you beyond the first obvious answers and gives the session a clear finish.

quiz.q: When do the most original ideas usually appear?
quiz.why: Obvious ideas come first, so the later ideas in a session are often the most original.

lessons.intro: You will learn to borrow solutions from fields far away from your own. It matters because problems that are hard in one field are often solved elegantly in another.

cards.b: Choose a field with little in common with your problem, such as biology, music or sport. The more distant the field, the more fresh solutions it can offer.
Ask how that field handles a similar challenge. Bees, for example, use a waggle dance to share the location of food with the rest of the hive.
Rewrite the solution in the language of your problem. The waggle idea might become a short visual signal that tells staff where to find a product.

fig.title: Matching fields to problems
fig.note: Each field offers a solution to a different problem.

ex.q: Ants leave scent trails to guide other ants to food. Which problem does this analogy best suit?
o: Guiding customers to the right shelf
ex.why: A scent trail marks a route that others can follow. That maps well onto guiding customers through a shop to the right shelf.

lessons.tip: Use the most distant field you can explain in one sentence.

quiz.q: What makes a distant field useful for ideas?
o: It has little in common with your problem
quiz.why: Distant fields offer solutions your own field would not normally consider.

quiz.q: What does translating an analogy back mean?
o: Rewriting the solution in your problem's terms
quiz.why: Translation turns a borrowed solution into a practical idea for your own setting.

lessons.t: Building idea maps from one centre
lessons.intro: You will learn to grow a map of related ideas outward from a central topic. It matters because a visual map shows the branches you can explore and the gaps you can fill.

cards.b: Write your topic in the middle of a blank page and draw a circle around it. A clear centre keeps every branch connected to the real problem.
Add four to six main branches for broad categories, such as people, place or cost. Each branch is a door to a set of related ideas.
Attach smaller ideas to each branch and draw lines between distant branches. Cross-links often create the combinations that produce new concepts.

fig.title: Idea map growth
fig.note: Each level multiplies the ideas by four.

ex.q: A map has 4 branches, and each branch has 3 twigs. How many twigs are there in total?
ex.why: Four branches each carrying three twigs gives 4 times 3. That equals 12 twigs in total.

lessons.tip: Use a different colour for each branch so the categories stand out.

quiz.q: Why should every branch connect back to the central topic?
o: To keep ideas linked to the real problem
To reduce the number of ideas
quiz.why: A clear centre keeps the whole map focused on the problem you are solving.

quiz.q: What do cross-links often create?
quiz.why: Linking distant branches joins ideas that were separate before, which is how new concepts emerge.

lessons.intro: You will learn to pick two unrelated objects and force them together into a new product. It matters because combining familiar things is one of the most reliable sources of new ideas.

cards.b: Choose two things that rarely meet, such as an umbrella and a lamp. Unrelated pairs force your mind to build a bridge instead of repeating a known product.
Write what each object does, how it looks and where it is used. Look for traits that might help one another, or that clash in an interesting way.
Describe the new object in one sentence. Ask who would buy it and what problem it solves, then decide whether it is worth a closer look.

fig.title: Forced connection steps
fig.note: Blend the traits, then give the new idea a clear name.

ex.q: A team joins a torch and a fan into one camping device. The torch has 2 light modes and the fan has 3 speeds. How many settings does the combined device have?
ex.why: Add the features together: 2 light modes and 3 fan speeds give 5 settings. The combined device therefore offers 5 settings in total.

lessons.tip: Name the combined idea before judging it, so it gets a fair hearing.

quiz.q: Why pick two unrelated objects?
o: They force a bridge that a known product would not
quiz.why: Unrelated pairs push the mind toward a new connection rather than a familiar product.

quiz.q: What should you do after blending the traits?
o: Give the idea a clear name
quiz.why: Naming the idea makes it concrete enough to discuss and assess.

lessons.intro: You will learn to take a useful feature from one product and place it into another. It matters because many successful products are improved versions of features borrowed from elsewhere.

cards.b: Write down the main features of a product you know well, such as its size, material, speed or price. Attributes are the parts you can move to something else.
Pick one attribute from a different product and transfer it to yours. A foldable shape from a camera might make a backpack easier to store.
Every borrowed attribute brings a cost. Ask what it makes easier, what it makes harder, and whether the trade is worth it for your users.

fig.title: Attribute transfer
fig.note: Borrowing one attribute changes how the product feels.

ex.q: A pen has a 14 cm body and a 2 cm cap. A designer adds a 3 cm extension borrowed from a torch. What is the new total length?
ex.why: Add the body, the cap and the extension: 14 plus 2 plus 3 equals 19 cm. The borrowed part adds length, so the total grows.

lessons.tip: Borrow from products your customers already understand well.

quiz.q: What is an attribute in this lesson?
o: A feature you can move from one product to another
quiz.why: Attributes are the concrete features, such as size or material, that can be transferred.

quiz.q: Why check the trade-off of a borrowed attribute?
o: Every borrowed feature has a cost
quiz.why: A borrowed feature may simplify one thing while making another harder, so the cost must be weighed.

lessons.intro: You will learn two SCAMPER moves, substitute and combine, to reshape a product or process. It matters because these two moves produce many practical improvements with little risk.

cards.b: Ask what could replace a component, a material or a step in the process. Swapping single-use paper for a reusable card can cut waste while keeping the same function.
Ask which two functions could merge into one item. The smartphone combined a camera, a music player and a phone, which shows how combining can reshape a market.
Apply one SCAMPER move at a time so you can see what each change does. Mixing all the moves at once makes the results hard to read.

fig.title: The SCAMPER letters
fig.note: Seven moves, each one a different way to change.

ex.q: A cafe replaces plastic straws with paper ones, and merges a coffee stand with a bookshop. Which two SCAMPER moves do these changes use?
ex.why: Replacing straws is Substitute, because one part is swapped for another. Merging two businesses is Combine, because two functions become one.

lessons.tip: Ask which part of your product you could swap before adding anything new.

quiz.q: Which SCAMPER move fits replacing a material with a reusable one?
quiz.why: Substitute means replacing a part, material or process with another option.

quiz.q: Why apply one SCAMPER move at a time?
o: So you can see what each change does
quiz.why: Testing one change at a time shows its effect clearly, while mixing changes hides cause and effect.

lessons.intro: You will learn to build a grid of options and combine one choice from each column. It matters because a small set of choices can create many distinct combinations.

cards.b: Break your product into three to five dimensions, such as material, power and shape. Each dimension becomes a column in your grid.
List three to five options for each dimension. Keep them specific, so each combination reads as a real product rather than a vague idea.
Choose one option from each column to form a combination. Work through several picks, and keep the ones that feel useful or surprising.

fig.title: A morphological box
fig.note: Pick one cell per row to build a combination.

ex.q: A box has 3 options for power, 3 options for shape and 4 options for glow. How many distinct combinations are possible, taking one option from each?
ex.why: Multiply the number of options in each column: 3 times 3 times 4. That equals 36 combinations.

lessons.tip: Score each combination quickly, and keep only the top few for deeper work.

quiz.q: What is each column in a morphological box?
quiz.why: Each column is one dimension, and its options are the choices for that dimension.

quiz.q: A box has 5 materials and 3 sizes. How many combinations are there?
quiz.why: Five materials times three sizes is 15 possible combinations.

lessons.intro: You will learn to combine two unrelated concepts into one idea using a simple blend. It matters because blended ideas can create new categories that neither concept suggests alone.

cards.b: Pick one concept from your field and one from a completely different area. Mixing a gym and a library, for example, can point toward a new kind of study space.
Describe the combined idea in a short phrase, such as a library you train in. Short phrases make the blend memorable and easy to test.
Identify the problem your blend could solve for a real person. If it solves nothing, adjust one of the concepts and try again.

fig.title: Two concepts make one
fig.note: Two concepts combine into one new idea.

ex.q: A library lends 120 books, and a gym lends 35 pieces of equipment. A library-gym blends the two and lends both. How many items does it lend in total?
ex.why: Add the two collections: 120 books plus 35 pieces of equipment. The blend therefore offers 155 items in total.

lessons.tip: Say the blend out loud, because awkward phrasing often hides a weak idea.

quiz.q: Why choose two distant concepts for a blend?
o: They can create a category neither suggests alone
quiz.why: Distant concepts produce combinations that are genuinely new rather than predictable.

quiz.q: What should you ask after writing a blend briefly?
o: What real problem it could solve
quiz.why: Testing whether the blend solves a real problem separates useful ideas from clever ones.

lessons.intro: You will learn to copy the structure or pattern of a natural system to solve a design problem. It matters because nature has tested many structures over very long periods.

cards.b: Pick a plant or animal that handles a challenge you face, such as shedding water or staying cool. Observe how its shape or pattern does the job.
Describe the principle behind the structure without the biology. A lotus leaf sheds water because its surface is covered in tiny bumps.
Use the principle in your design. A surface texture that repels water could be applied to a coat, a window or a kitchen tile.

fig.title: Nature to design
fig.note: Copy the principle, not the exact biology.

ex.q: A lotus leaf has bumps that repel water. A coat designer adds bumps to 40 square centimetres of fabric, then adds 25 more. How much textured area is there in total?
ex.why: Add the two areas: 40 plus 25 equals 65 square centimetres. The total textured area is the sum of both patches.

lessons.tip: Name the principle in plain words before you look for a technical solution.

quiz.q: What should you copy from a natural structure?
quiz.why: The principle transfers to other settings, while the full biology usually is not needed for your design.

quiz.q: What does the lotus leaf principle suggest for a window?
quiz.why: The bumpy surface sheds water, so a similar texture could help a window stay cleaner.

lessons.intro: You will learn to combine two conflicting constraints into one fresh rule. It matters because a strong constraint can spark a design that a free brief would never produce.

cards.b: Write down each constraint your problem has, such as a low budget or a tight deadline. Constraints feel like limits, but they also shape what you can make.
Place two constraints side by side that seem to fight each other, such as fast and very quiet. Their clash often reveals an unusual rule.
Create a single rule that respects both constraints, for example make the noise short and well timed. This rule can become your design brief.

fig.title: Options left after constraints
fig.note: Each constraint narrows the options but sharpens focus.

ex.q: A project starts with 20 possible designs. A budget limit removes 9 designs and a deadline removes 4 more. How many designs remain?
ex.why: Start with 20, then subtract 9 and then 4. That leaves 7 designs to consider.

lessons.tip: Treat every constraint as a design input rather than a complaint.

quiz.q: Why pair two constraints that conflict?
o: Their clash can reveal an unusual rule
quiz.why: A clash forces a creative compromise, which often produces a rule nobody considered.

quiz.q: What does a constraint do to your options?
quiz.why: Each constraint removes some options, which makes the remaining ones easier to focus on.

lessons.intro: You will learn a simple scoring method to rate how new and useful a combined idea is. It matters because novelty alone is not enough, since an idea also has to work.

cards.b: Give each idea a score from one to five for how new it is and how useful it is. Scoring turns a vague feeling into a comparison you can use.
Multiply the novelty score by the usefulness score to get a combined rating out of 25. Ideas that score high on both rise to the top quickly.
An idea with a perfect novelty score and a score of one for usefulness is a curiosity, not a product. Look for balanced scores before you invest time.

fig.title: Combined scores out of 25
fig.note: Idea B balances novelty and usefulness best.

ex.q: One idea scores 4 for novelty and 5 for usefulness. Another scores 5 for novelty and 2 for usefulness. Which has the higher combined score?
ex.why: Multiply each pair: 4 times 5 is 20, and 5 times 2 is 10. The first idea therefore scores higher, at 20.

lessons.tip: Score ideas after a short break so your first reaction does not dominate.

quiz.q: What is the highest possible combined score in this method?
quiz.why: The maximum is five times five, which equals 25.

quiz.q: Why avoid ideas with an extreme score on one side only?
o: They are curiosities rather than workable products
quiz.why: A high novelty score with low usefulness rarely becomes a practical product.

lessons.t: Why most first ideas need testing
lessons.intro: You will learn why your first version of an idea almost always needs testing before you rely on it. It matters because untested ideas can waste time, money and goodwill.

cards.b: Even strong ideas usually change after contact with real users. Expect your first version to be a starting point rather than a finished answer.
Most ideas rest on assumptions about what people want or can afford. Testing exposes which assumptions are true and which are wrong.
A small test costs a fraction of a full launch. Finding a flaw early saves the effort you would otherwise spend on the wrong version.

fig.title: Relative cost to fix a flaw
fig.note: Flaws found later cost far more to fix.

ex.q: A flaw costs 1 unit to fix at sketch stage, 5 at prototype stage and 20 at launch. How many more units does fixing it at launch cost than at prototype stage?
ex.why: Subtract the prototype cost from the launch cost: 20 minus 5 equals 15. Fixing it late costs 15 units more.

lessons.tip: Ask what would prove this idea wrong, then go and look for that evidence.

quiz.q: What do untested assumptions often do?
quiz.why: Assumptions can conceal risks until real users reveal them, often late and at great expense.

quiz.q: Why do small tests help?
o: They cost less than a full launch
quiz.why: A small test uses fewer resources, so a flaw found there is cheaper to fix.

lessons.intro: You will learn to write your idea as a single sentence that names the user, the problem and the benefit. It matters because a clear statement is easy to test and easy to explain.

cards.b: Start with who the idea is for, such as busy parents or night-shift nurses. A specific user makes the idea easier to shape and to judge.
Describe the problem they face and the benefit your idea gives them. Keep the sentence short enough to say in one breath.
If the statement needs a second sentence, the idea is probably two ideas. Split it, then test each part separately.

fig.title: Idea statement parts
fig.note: Fill each part, then read the whole sentence aloud.

ex.q: A statement reads: night-shift nurses sleep 2 extra hours after each shift using a blackout cover. If a nurse works 5 shifts a week, how many extra sleep hours does she gain in a week?
ex.why: Five shifts at 2 extra hours each gives 5 times 2. That equals 10 extra sleep hours per week.

lessons.tip: If you cannot say the idea in one sentence, it is not yet clear enough to test.

quiz.q: What should a one-line idea statement name?
o: The user, the problem and the benefit
quiz.why: Naming these three parts gives the idea a clear shape that can be tested.

quiz.q: What does it mean if your statement needs two sentences?
o: It may be two ideas to split and test
quiz.why: Two sentences often signal two separate ideas, which are easier to test one at a time.

lessons.intro: You will learn to choose low-cost tests that answer your biggest question before you spend heavily. It matters because the cheapest answer to a risky question is usually the best one to get first.

cards.b: Find the assumption that would sink the idea if it were false. That question deserves a test before anything else gets built.
Choose a test that answers the question with the least money and time, such as a survey, a landing page or a short trial. Cheap tests keep your options open.
Write down what result would count as success before you run the test. This stops you reading the outcome to fit what you hoped for.

fig.title: Cheap test loop
fig.note: Repeat the loop for each major assumption.

ex.q: A team shows a landing page to 100 visitors. Success means at least 15 sign-ups. 18 visitors sign up. Is the test a success?
ex.why: The rule was at least 15 sign-ups, and 18 is more than that. The test therefore counts as a success.

lessons.tip: Spend your first hour on the question most likely to kill the idea.

quiz.q: Which assumption should you test first?
o: The one that would sink the idea if false
quiz.why: Testing the riskiest assumption first prevents wasted effort on an idea that cannot work.

quiz.q: Why decide the success result before testing?
o: To stop you reading results to fit your hopes
quiz.why: A success rule set in advance keeps the judgement honest when the results come in.

lessons.intro: You will learn to set clear criteria and weights before judging several ideas. It matters because judging without criteria tends to favour whichever idea you liked first.

cards.b: Write down the criteria that define a good idea for your situation, such as cost, speed and appeal. Keep the list between three and five items.
Give the most important criterion a higher weight, such as double the others. Weights stop a minor factor from outvoting a major one.
Rate every idea against each criterion on the same scale. Consistent scoring makes the comparison fair and reveals the real strengths.

fig.title: Scores out of five
fig.note: Cost is weighted double, so it counts most.

ex.q: Cost is weighted 2 and speed is weighted 1. Alpha scores 3 for cost and 4 for speed. What is Alpha's weighted total?
ex.why: Multiply the cost score by its weight: 3 times 2 gives 6. Add the speed score of 4 to make 10.

lessons.tip: Write the criteria down before you look at any of the ideas.

quiz.q: Why give important criteria a higher weight?
o: To make the sheet look busy
So a minor factor cannot outvote a major one
quiz.why: Weights keep the scoring aligned with what matters most in your situation.

quiz.q: What is a good number of criteria?
quiz.why: Three to five criteria cover the essentials without making the judgement hard to manage.

lessons.intro: You will learn to build quick, rough versions of an idea to test with people. It matters because a rough prototype shows how people use an idea far faster than a finished product can.

cards.b: Use paper, cardboard, sticky notes or a basic drawing. Rough materials signal that the idea can change, so people give more honest feedback.
Build only the steps a user must take to get the main benefit. Leaving out the extras keeps the work fast and focuses the test on what matters.
Hand the prototype to a person and watch them try to use it without help. Where they hesitate or get stuck reveals the real problems.

fig.title: Versions get better
fig.note: Each version fixes the problems found in the last.

ex.q: A team runs two rounds of paper prototype tests. Round one finds 12 problems and round two finds 5 more. Fixing each problem takes 2 hours. How many hours does fixing all 17 problems take?
ex.why: Add the problems: 12 plus 5 equals 17. At 2 hours each, 17 problems take 34 hours.

lessons.tip: Build the prototype in under an hour, so it stays cheap to throw away.

quiz.q: Why keep prototypes rough?
o: To signal the idea can change and invite honest feedback
quiz.why: Rough materials make people feel free to criticise, which gives more useful feedback.

quiz.q: What should you do while a person uses the prototype?
quiz.why: Watching reveals where people hesitate, which explanations would otherwise hide.

lessons.t: Asking five users what they would do
lessons.intro: You will learn how to test an idea with a small group of real users by asking them to show, not tell. It matters because what people say they would do often differs from what they actually do.

cards.b: Find five people who match your target user, rather than friends who want to be kind. A small group of the right people reveals most of the main problems.
Ask what they did the last time they faced the problem, not whether they would use your idea. Past actions predict future behaviour far better than promises.
Note each problem that appears for two or more users. Patterns across people matter more than a single strong opinion.

fig.title: Users who hit each problem
fig.note: Problems seen by several users deserve attention first.

ex.q: Five users test a prototype. Four hit a slow setup, three hit a price doubt and one hits a lost login. How many user-problem reports are there in total?
ex.why: Add the reports: 4 plus 3 plus 1 equals 8. Each report counts once, so the total is 8 user-problem reports.

lessons.tip: Stay quiet after asking a question, because silence often draws out the real answer.

quiz.q: Why ask about past behaviour?
o: Past actions predict behaviour better than promises
quiz.why: What people actually did is a stronger guide than what they say they might do.

quiz.q: Which problem deserves attention first?
o: One seen by a single user
quiz.why: Problems repeated across several users point to a genuine pattern worth fixing.

lessons.intro: You will learn to read the signals from small experiments and decide whether to continue. It matters because a small group of results can mislead you if you read it carelessly.

cards.b: Compare your test result against the success rule you set in advance. A large gap is a stronger signal than a small wobble.
Ten results can swing wildly by chance. Treat early results as hints, and run more trials before making a big decision.
Ask why the result happened, not just whether it did. A surprising result often points to a better version of the idea.

fig.title: Trial results in a row
fig.note: Watch the trend, not any single result.

ex.q: In round one, 6 of 10 users complete a task. In round two, 9 of 10 complete it. What percentage of the 20 users completed the task overall?
ex.why: Add the completions: 6 plus 9 gives 15. Fifteen out of 20 is 75 percent.

lessons.tip: Write down the exact number of users before you describe any result.

quiz.q: Why treat early results as hints?
o: Small numbers can swing by chance
quiz.why: With few results, chance can create large swings that disappear with more trials.

quiz.q: What is a stronger question to ask about a surprising result?
quiz.why: Understanding the cause often points to a better version of the idea.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to drop an idea the evidence does not support, without losing the lessons it taught. It matters because clinging to weak ideas wastes time that could go to better ones.

cards.b: Set in advance what evidence would stop the idea, such as fewer than a set number of sign-ups. A stopping rule removes emotion from the decision.
Before you drop an idea, write down what the test taught you. Those lessons often shape the next idea more than the idea itself.
Stopping an idea early is a success because it frees time. Name the decision as good judgement, so people feel safe proposing bold ideas.

fig.title: Keep or stop an idea
fig.note: Set the rule before the results arrive.

ex.q: A stopping rule says to stop if fewer than 30 people sign up from 100 visitors. Only 22 sign up. What should happen?
ex.why: 22 is fewer than 30, which breaks the rule. The stopping rule therefore says to stop the idea.

lessons.tip: Keep a short file of stopped ideas so their lessons can be reused.

quiz.q: Why set a stopping rule in advance?
o: To remove emotion from the decision
quiz.why: A rule written in advance stops attachment from overriding the evidence.

quiz.q: What is worth saving from a stopped idea?
quiz.why: Lessons from a test often shape stronger ideas later.

lessons.t: Iterating a promising idea in rounds
lessons.intro: You will learn to improve a promising idea through short, repeated rounds of change and testing. It matters because most strong ideas are refined rather than perfect on the first attempt.

cards.b: Alter a single element each time, such as the price, the wording or the layout. Changing one thing makes it clear which change caused any improvement.
Record the change, the result and the decision after each round. A log stops you repeating failed changes and shows the path you have taken.
When rounds stop producing meaningful gains, the idea is as good as it is likely to get. Move on to a new test or to delivery.

fig.title: Iteration rounds
fig.note: Keep each round short so learning stays fast.

ex.q: Round one lifts sign-ups from 10 to 14. Round two lifts them from 14 to 17. How many extra sign-ups were gained across both rounds?
ex.why: Round one gained 4 and round two gained 3. Together they add 7 extra sign-ups, which matches going from 10 to 17.

lessons.tip: Set a fixed number of rounds before you start, so the work does not drift.

quiz.q: Why change only one thing per round?
o: To see which change caused the improvement
Because only one change is allowed
To keep the design the same
quiz.why: Single changes make cause and effect clear, while several at once hide which one worked.

quiz.q: When should you stop iterating?
o: When gains become small and meaningful improvement stops
quiz.why: Diminishing returns signal that the idea has reached its practical limit for now.

lessons.t: Turning a tested idea into a plan
lessons.intro: You will learn to turn a tested idea into a plan with clear steps, owners and dates. It matters because a good idea creates value only when someone turns it into action.

cards.b: Write one short paragraph that states what you tested and what you found. This summary keeps the plan honest about what is known and what is still uncertain.
List the actions needed to move from test to delivery, and place them in order. Each step should have one owner and a clear finish point.
Give each step a date and schedule a short review to check progress. Regular check-ins catch slipping work before it becomes a crisis.

fig.title: From test to delivery
fig.note: Each stage builds on the one before it.

ex.q: A plan has 5 steps, each taking 3 days, followed by a 2-day review. How many days does the plan take in total?
ex.why: The five steps take 5 times 3, which is 15 days. Adding the 2-day review gives 17 days in total.

lessons.tip: Assign one owner to each step, because shared responsibility often means no one acts.

quiz.q: Why should each step have one owner?
o: So responsibility is clear and not diffused
quiz.why: Single ownership prevents steps from falling between people who each assume someone else will act.

quiz.q: What does a short check-in catch?
o: Slipping work before it becomes a crisis
quiz.why: Regular reviews reveal delays early, while there is still time to correct them.
